title: Imam al-Shafi'i
hookLine: a descendant of the Prophet's clan, who studied with Malik and the Hanafis

cards: A young man arrives in Medina already knowing a book by heart. It's Malik's Muwatta, and the story goes that he memorized it before he ever met its author. He sits in Malik's circle and reads it back to him.
Years later he's in Iraq, reading the books of al-Shaybani, Abu Hanifa's student, and arguing with the Hanafis face to face. Medina's way and Kufa's way both pass through one mind.
What comes out is a third school, and a new way of asking how law should be found at all.

teach.h: OF QURAYSH, AN ORPHAN IN MECCA.
teach.b: His name is Muhammad ibn Idris, called al-Shafi'i after an ancestor named Shafi'.
He was of Quraysh, the Prophet's tribe, from the line of al-Muttalib, a brother of Hashim, who was great-grandfather to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. So the two family trees meet a few generations back.
Yet his biographers say he grew up an orphan, poor, in Mecca, with a mother who couldn't afford paper.

teach.h: MALIK IN MEDINA, THE HANAFIS IN IRAQ.
teach.b: He learned the Qur'an and Arabic in Mecca, then studied with Malik in Medina. Later, in Iraq, he studied the Hanafi books, and tradition says he learned from al-Shaybani in person.
He had sat with the imam of Medina and read the people of reasoned judgment closely: learned from both.
He didn't simply blend them. He asked what each was doing and why, and wrote it down as a method. From Malik he kept the hadith at the center; from the Hanafis, careful reasoning.
He argued with both, and ended his days in Egypt, where his tomb stands in Cairo.

teach.h: A WEEK OF TWO SCHOOLS, AND A THIRD.
teach.b: Look back over these days: two times for Asr, a judge's seat refused, I don't know in Medina, the well-trodden path, the living practice, hands at the sides.
Now a student who carried Kufa and Medina, and asked how they fit. The Qur'an gives a short line for students like him: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.

how: Shafi'i Muslims, across places such as Egypt, East Africa, Yemen and Southeast Asia, follow the school of Imam al-Shafi'i, who studied with Malik in Medina and with Hanafi scholars in Iraq.

games.q: you've memorized Malik's book and now you're in Iraq, among the Hanafis, who reason differently. what do you do?
o: leave: Malik already gave you everything.

games.why: he studied their books, argued with them, and came out with a method of his own that drew on both.

practice: Bring to mind two people who taught you the same thing in different ways: two grandparents cooking the same dish, two coaches, a parent who explained and a parent who showed.

Notice what each got right, where they disagreed, and how much of each is in what you do today. If you pray, you can say the line from Surah Ta Ha, My Lord! Increase me in knowledge; if not, simply rest with both faces in mind.
